L12: # About the security of 1Password for Agents
L13: 
L14: About the security of 1Password for Agents Learn about the security of connecting 1Password with your agents.Security and privacy 1Password features
L15: 
L16: 【1†1Password for Agents】 allows you to authorize agents to securely use items from your 1Password account. Agents can request that individual items be filled, and with your approval, the 1Password extension in the agent developer’s browser fills those items directly into a website on your behalf.
L17: 1Password for Agents is available for 【2†Login items】, including one-time password codes, saved in your 【3†Personal】 or 【4†Private】 vault.
L18: 
L19: This article describes the security model of 1Password for Agents and the risks associated with it.
L20: ## Security model
L21: 
L22: The security of 1Password for Agents builds upon the fundamental 【5†1Password security model】.
L23: 
L24: 1Password for Agents splits the material needed to decrypt an item between the agent and 1Password. When you connect an agent, 1Password creates a new keyset for the connection and encrypts it with a new integration key, which only the agent developer receives.
L25: When you approve an item, 1Password locally derives a new “client” key from your vault key. 1Password encrypts the vault key for the approved item with the client key, and the agent developer receives an encrypted copy of the client key.
L26: 
L27: To fill an item, the agent developer uses its integration key to decrypt the connection’s keyset, decrypts the client key, and sends the client key to 【6†1Password’s confidential computing enclave】, where it’s used to decrypt your vault key.
L28: Inside the enclave, the vault key is used to decrypt the requested item. The item is then provided to the 1Password extension directly, running inside the agent’s hosted browser runtime.

L12: # Use 1Password to sign in to sites with supported agents
L13: 
L14: Use 1Password to sign in to sites with supported agents Learn how to use 1Password to fill logins when your personal agent needs to sign in.Agents Get started
L15: 
L16: Some tasks you may want to delegate to your personal agent require signing in to complete, like booking a flight, making an appointment, or shopping for groceries. 1Password can fill your logins when your agent needs to sign in, so you don’t have to share your passwords with the agent.
L17: With 1Password for Agents, you can:
L18:   * Let your agent use 1Password to complete tasks that require signing in. 1Password fills your username, password, and one-time passwords directly into the website’s sign-in form in the agent’s browser, so you don’t need to enter them in the agent’s chat.
L19:   * Stay in control of what your agent can access. 1Password shows you which agent is asking to sign in and suggested logins for the website. You review the request and choose whether to approve.
L20:   * Access your logins from one trusted place across multiple agents. Store all the logins you want your agents to use in 1Password, so your passwords stay organized and protected in one place and you can adopt new agents without starting over.
L21:   * Change your mind any time. Disconnect the integration when you no longer want an agent to sign in with 1Password.
L22: When 1Password fills a login, the agent app makes sure the agent can’t see the sign-in page. Learn more about 【1†how 1Password fills your logins】 and 【2†how 1Password and the agent protect your credentials】.
L23: #### Tip
L24: 
L25: 1Password for Agents is opt-in only. You’ll need to connect 1Password to a supported agent to use this feature. Don’t see your agent? 【3†Join the waitlist†1password.com】 to be notified when more agents are supported.

L2: Thursday, October 22, 2026 9:00am EDT
L3: # 1Password for Agents Launches as the Trust Layer for Personal AI Agents
L4: 
L5: 
L6: 
L7: New platform lets personal AI agents sign in and complete tasks securely without seeing or storing passwords, secrets, or credentials
L8: TORONTO — 【1†1Password】, a leader in identity security, today announced 1Password for Agents, a new platform that helps personal AI agents safely use the passwords, secrets, and credentials they need to complete approved tasks without seeing or storing them. 1Password for Agents lets people keep the credentials secure in 1Password while safely enabling personal AI agents to sign in and get things done on their behalf.
L9: 1Password is designed to support people’s AI agents of choice, and is building with companies across the personal AI agent ecosystem, including Muse, from Meta, Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI, SpaceXSI Grok Bot, and Town Townie.
L10: Personal AI agents are moving beyond answering questions to proactively planning family vacations, managing recurring bills, and preparing expense reports. Whether for personal or work tasks, agents need access to accounts and sensitive information people already use. Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time.
L11: 1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.
L12: “Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf. The old model where you hand over a credential and hope for the best doesn’t work,” said Aashish Tripathi, Chief Product Officer at 1Password. “An agent should be able to do the job it’s been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account, and 1Password provides the trust layer that makes this possible across personal agent experiences.”

L16: # Introduction
L17: ## Data Provenance without Compromising Privacy, That is Why!【8†​】
L18: 
L19: The Internet currently lacks effective, privacy-preserving Data Provenance. 【9†TLS†en.wikipedia.org】, also known as the "s" in "https" 🔐 to the general public, ensures that data can be securely communicated between a server and a user. But how can this user credibly share this data with another user or server without compromising security, privacy, and control?
L20: Enter TLSNotary: a protocol enabling users to export data securely from any website. Using Zero Knowledge Proof (ZKP) technology, this data can be selectively shared with others in a cryptographically verifiable manner.
L21: 
L22: TLSNotary makes data truly portable and allows a user, the `Prover`, to share it with another party, the `Verifier`, as they see fit.
L23: ## How Does the TLSNotary Protocol Work?【10†​】
L24: 
L25: The TLSNotary protocol consists of 3 steps:
L26: 
L27:   1. The `Prover` requests data from a `Server` over TLS while cooperating with the `Verifier` in secure and privacy-preserving multi-party computation (MPC).
L28:   2. The `Prover` selectively discloses the data to the `Verifier`.
L29:   3. The `Verifier` verifies the data.
L30: 
L31: 【11†Image】 【12†Image】
L32: ### ① Multi-party TLS Request【13†​】
L33: 
L34: TLSNotary works by adding a third party, a `Verifier`, to the usual TLS connection between the `Prover` and a `Server`. This `Verifier` is not "【14†a man in the middle†en.wikipedia.org】". Instead, the `Verifier` participates in a secure multi-party computation (MPC) to jointly operate the TLS connection without seeing the data in plain text. By participating in the MPC, the `Verifier` can validate the authenticity of the data the `Prover` received from the `Server`.
L35: The TLSNotary protocol is transparent to the `Server`. From the `Server`'s perspective, the `Prover`'s connection is a standard TLS connection.

L926: ### Site Agent access policy
L927: 
L928: Today, an Agent infers a Site’s rules by trying something and interpreting the Site response (usually, whether it gets blocked). That wastes resources on both sides, and in some cases makes honest Agents appear to be malicious. Robots.txt says where a crawler may go, but isn’t fully suited to express what Agents may do.
L929: Sites need a machine-readable way to publish what actions Agents are allowed to do. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is actively working on some preference expression mechanisms for this, primarily in the 【820†AI Preferences Working Group†datatracker.ietf.org】. However, the focus of the group is on expressing preferences for use (such as training, inference, and search), and there is still not a group focused on the larger need for preference expression mechanisms discussed here.
L930: ### On open source and local Agents
L931: 
L932: Agents that are not run as an “Intermediary” (e.g. on-device Agents, or locally hosted Agents such as OpenClaw) raise different concerns. Primarily, they look like (and are) automation, and they have no single party to build reputation or hold accountability with.
L933: 
L934: There are many solutions to this, one of which is to ask these Agents to provide a Unique ID. However, addressing this is not the initial focus of Trusted Agent Delegation.
L935: ## What’s next
L936: Real-world solutions to the problems that Sites face won’t emerge from fragmented, vendor-specific mechanisms. They require open, interoperable standards that are rooted in real world experience.
L937: We have been, and continue to actively collaborate across the ecosystem, with major Operators, identity verification companies, payment providers, merchants, publishers, proxy providers, and cloud browsing companies, to align operational requirements directly with active work on these problems in the IETF and elsewhere
L938: Our focus is on bridging the gap between running code and emerging specifications across working groups and activities like Web Bot Auth, AIPREFs, OAuth, WIMSE, and MOLE. We are doing this, in part, by co-authoring and refining open protocols like WBA and MOLE and building and deploying implementations of these protocols at scale.
L939: We are also announcing the 【821†Trusted Agent Delegation†trustedagentdelegation.org】 (TAD) coalition. The goal of TAD is to bring a group of representatives across the ecosystem to have discussions on the overall problem set that was put forth in this document, examine all existing protocols, and then to bring more well-defined problems or problems to the IETF to work through, as needed. We intend to hold side meetings at the IETF and workshops in the future to facilitate discussion.
L940: If you are building agents, agent runtimes, running an edge or cloud platform, or managing commercial or compliance applications or infrastructure, we need you to get involved in these efforts too. Check out 【821†this page†trustedagentdelegation.org】 for more information on how to participate.
L941: ## What you can do today
L942: 
L943: An open, interoperable foundation  is where we're headed, starting with TAD. But you don't have to wait for new protocols to start regaining visibility and control. As of 【822†this week】, Cloudflare customers can take three concrete steps:
L944: See which Agents are on your site, and what they're doing. 【823†Security Analytics†dash.cloudflare.com】 now breaks out Personal Assistants as their own traffic category, and a new widget lists every Agent visiting your site, how many requests each one sends, the paths it hits, and the errors it runs into. Unexplained automated traffic becomes traffic you can reason about.
L945: And for the broader picture of AI crawlers and bots affect your business, including how much each Operator crawls versus the traffic it sends back, Enterprise Bot Management customers can use 【824†Business Insights†developers.cloudflare.com】.
L946: Set access on your terms, per Agent. Using 【825†AI Crawler and Agent access policies†dash.cloudflare.com】, you can welcome the Agents that bring you business and restrict the ones that don't — allow an Agent across your site, block it only on pages with ads, or block it entirely. Your Search and Training policies stay independent.
L947: Tie an Agent back to the user it acts for — and act on it. For sites using 【826†Account Abuse Protection†developers.cloudflare.com】 (early access), every login and sign-up now shows whether a personal Agent made the request, and which one. When an attacker abuses a shared Agent on one account, you can mitigate that account — with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID — without blocking the Agent for every other legitimate user behind it.

L1383: A record stating that a teardown processed a set of descendants establishes that its signer made that statement. It does not establish that the set was every descendant at the relevant boundary, that every write persisted, or that nothing was issued concurrently. A claim that a set is complete MUST state the basis on which it is complete, and a verifier that cannot establish that basis MUST report not established with the coverage limb named, rather than reading the claim as covering the whole set.

L2578:     A successor to an office or a sponsor is treated as holding the predecessor's whole delegation tree, or a restore brings back authority that had ended. L2584:     An adapter carries an authority artifact into another stack and the dimensions that stack has no member for are dropped rather than reported as unsupported. L3361: Authority question. Can a verifier read an empty window in an evidence store as a finding that nothing happened in that window?【1923†¶】
L3362: Pressure this case puts on an authority model. An evidence store read inside its own delivery lag is not a complete account of the interval asked about, so a model that reconstructs authority state at a past instant has to say what an empty window is worth. The corpus records delivery lag as a bound a deployment declares and monitors, and it does not follow that an enforcement decision waits on its own audit record.【1924†¶】
L3363: What a naive implementation gets wrong. Treating an empty audit-log window as proof nothing happened during that window, when it may only mean the batched delivery hasn't caught up yet, exactly the wrong conclusion for an investigation happening in near-real-time.【1925†¶】
